candidates.title: United by the Economy, Divided by Convictions: Is the Economic Vote Affected by Polarisation in Latin America?
candidates.abstract: This paper examines how political polarisation conditions the relationship between economic performance and electoral outcomes. While a large literature shows that voters tend to reward incumbents for good economic conditions and punish them for poor performance, these effects are far from universal, as polarisation functions as a contextual moderator of economic voting by altering how voters interpret economic information. We develop a formal theoretical model in which increasing polarisation expands the share of voters who are unresponsive to economic performance, reducing the economic accountability of voting. We test the model's predictions using data from 62 presidential elections in 16 Latin American countries between 1994 and 2019. The empirical analysis shows that public spending increases and inflation decreases incumbent reelection probability in low-polarisation contexts, consistent with standard economic voting models. However, these effects weaken significantly as polarisation rises and become statistically insignificant at high levels of polarisation. These findings suggest that polarisation systematically reshapes the mechanisms of electoral accountability by reducing voters' responsiveness to economic conditions. More broadly, the results highlight a trade-off inherent in democratic competition: while some degree of political polarisation may structure political choice, excessive levels of polarisation undermine the capacity of elections to discipline incumbents based on performance.

candidates.title: Transparency Is Not Enough: Political Identity and the Acceptance of AI-Generated Governance Information
candidates.abstract: Political transparency promotes accountability only if citizens are willing to accept the information provided. As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly mediates the production and evaluation of public information, an important question is whether AI-generated political information remains subject to partisan filtering. We examine this question using an online survey experiment in Taiwan that varies two potential partisan cues surrounding an AI-generated legislative-performance evaluation: the partisan camp of the legislator receiving a favorable evaluation and the partisan alignment of the media outlet associated with the AI system. The results show that acceptance is strongly shaped by congruence with the favorably evaluated legislator. Respondents are more accepting when the legislator belongs to their own partisan camp and substantially less accepting when the legislator belongs to an opposing camp. By contrast, congruence with the media outlet associated with the AI system has no statistically significant effect. Further, prior generative-AI usage is positively associated with acceptance, but this association is significantly weaker when the favorably evaluated legislator is politically congruent with the respondent. These findings demonstrate that AI-mediated transparency does not eliminate partisan filtering and suggest that the partisan implications of AI-generated outputs may matter more than the political alignment of the institutions associated with their production.

candidates.title: Trump’s Second Presidency: A Public Perspective
candidates.abstract: Donald Trump’s second presidency has generated intense controversy among policymakers, investors, and the public. Existing research has largely examined specific policies or measured public opinion through surveys distinguishing support from opposition. Using Google Trends data from January 2025 to September 2026, this study examines the drivers of public attention to Trump, associated political narratives, and cross-national spillover. First, attention peaks are associated with major political events and policy developments, including executive actions, immigration, government restructuring, trade disputes, social policies, and international conflicts. Second, opposition-oriented narratives exhibit a more consistent relation with overall attention to Trump than supporter-oriented narratives, such as Make America Great Again, America First, and religiously framed support, whose associations vary across political circumstances. Third, there are different patterns of political attention spillover. In Australia, Trump-related attention has a stronger and more persistent predictive relation with Pauline Hanson than with Anthony Albanese. In the United Kingdom, the corresponding relations with Nigel Farage and Keir Starmer are broadly similar, although their lag structures differ. These findings suggest that political attention spillovers depend on both ideological affinity and domestic political and diplomatic contexts. This study offers a novel framework for examining public attention beyond conventional measures of political approval and provides a foundation for future research on public narratives, policy preferences, and government decision-making.

candidates.title: Learning from Abroad? Citizen Preferences for International Policy Models
candidates.abstract: Politicians and policy professionals frequently refer to successful examples abroad to justify and promote policy reforms, making international comparisons central to policy debates. Yet we know little about which countries citizens prefer their own country to learn from, and whether information about policy performance changes those preferences. We study these questions using a cross-national survey in six countries in which respondents repeatedly choose between pairs of countries as policy models for the economy, immigration, and climate change. To identify the causal effect of performance information, we embed a randomized experiment in which half see country names only, while the other half also see issue-specific performance rankings. Citizens favor well-governed and affluent countries as policy models. Performance information shifts preferences toward better-performing countries, especially for the economy, with smaller effects for immigration and climate change. These findings contribute to understanding the micro-foundations of international policy learning.

candidates.title: State Atrocities, Rebel Governance, and Public Opinion on Humanitarian Intervention
candidates.abstract: How do rebel groups shape democratic publics’ attitudes toward humanitarian intervention? Many state-led atrocities occur during civil wars, yet rebels are often portrayed solely as sources of instability rather than as governing actors who shape external perceptions. We argue that rebels’ modes of governance—whether inclusive or exclusive in service provision and decision-making—fundamentally shape public opinion on intervention. Inclusive governance that embodies equality and participation reinforces identification with democratic values, strengthening the moral imperative to protect and the instrumental confidence that intervention would be both justified and effective. In contrast, exclusive governance, marked by coercion or discrimination, undermines perceptions of shared identity and moral legitimacy, making state repression appear justified and intervention less defensible. We test these claims through survey experiments in the U.S. (N=1,615) and the U.K. (N=1,583). Across both countries, inclusive governance boosts perceived legitimacy and credibility of rebels, fostering positive attitudes toward humanitarian intervention, while exclusive governance undermines these perceptions and weakens public endorsement.

candidates.title: How Different are Different Differences-in-Differences? A Large-Scale Meta-Analysis -- by Peter Hull
candidates.abstract: I use AI-assisted replication to assess the empirical importance of negative weights in two-way fixed effects (TWFE) estimation, drawing on 1,346 staggered-adoption specifications from 108 economics papers. TWFE estimates are highly correlated with estimates from modern difference-in-differences methods, with observed sign reversals in 10.8–14.5% of comparisons and greater precision for TWFE. Hierarchical models that account for estimation noise imply a 91–98% correlation between estimands and a 0.6–2.1% probability of obtaining a statistically significant TWFE estimate with the opposite sign from the modern estimand. These findings suggest negative weights may be a less serious problem in practice, and illustrate how AI can support large-scale empirical assessments of new econometric methods.

candidates.title: Flooded by China? Trade diversion due to US tariffs during Trump’s first mandate
candidates.abstract: This paper investigates whether US tariffs on China diverted Chinese exports towards the EU, exploiting the first US-China trade war as a setting that permits clean identification of trade diversion effects. Applying difference-in-differences local projections to highly disaggregated tariff, import and unit value data, it shows that trade diversion occurred but was limited in size. For each dollar reduction in US imports from China, 9 cents were redirected to the EU market in real terms. The effects varied substantially across products and destination markets. Trade diversion was strongest for complex capital goods and homogeneous intermediate inputs, and was more pronounced in EU markets with greater import exposure to China and weaker competition from alternative suppliers. Products experiencing effective diversion also exhibited significant price declines, with competitive pressures concentrated in lower-price market segments. These findings suggest that tariffs of a magnitude comparable to those imposed by the United States in 2025 could redirect Chinese exports towards the EU, potentially contributing to a second “China shock” in Europe. While the aggregate effects are modest, diversion and price pressures may be considerably stronger in specific product categories and destination markets.

candidates.title: Visual presentation raises trust in election polls
candidates.abstract: Election polls are arguably the most visible signals of public opinion in modern democracies, yet how the design of poll reports shapes their appeal, perceived credibility, and informational value has not been systematically studied. In a preregistered visual conjoint experiment conducted during the 2025 German federal election campaign, 22,658 voters evaluated poll reports varying across format, reference values, and technical information, in 160 possible designs. All visual formats were rated as more attractive and trustworthy than text-only reports. Trust gains were greatest among respondents with lower data and polling literacy and less accurate beliefs about current polling, whereas the appeal of visualization was greatest among the most literate. Disclosing the margin of error made reports less attractive without affecting trust, and no format made expectations about the election outcome more accurate. Text, the dominant format in poll coverage, is thus the least effective at fostering trust and accessibility.

candidates.title: Mobile Value, Anchored Burden: The Value–Burden Lock-in in Transition-Mineral Value Chains
candidates.abstract: The global transition toward cleaner energy has sharply increased demand for energy transition minerals, intensifying concerns about supply security. Less attention has been paid to how the benefits and burdens of this transition are distributed across countries. This paper proposes two related concepts, mobile value and anchored burden, to help explain why mineral-rich countries in the Global South capture little of the value their minerals generate while bearing much of the cost of extracting them. Mobile value describes how processing, and the value it generates, tends to concentrate where capabilities, capital, and market power reside rather than where minerals are mined. Anchored burden describes how geology fixes where extraction and its local damage occur, so that where the capacity to regulate is limited, the burden stays with mining communities. Together, the two can produce a value–burden lock-in, in which low value capture and a concentrated externality burden reinforce each other, a condition that price volatility and geopolitical risk can tighten. The Indonesian case adds a caution, which we call the upgrading double bind: bringing processing onshore does not by itself mean that the value stays in the country. We argue that, because value rises at each stage of the chain while the externality cost stays at the mine, extraction-stage countries can end up with a net cost, whereas the economies that capture the highest-value stages can retain a net benefit. We illustrate these concepts with global reserve, refining, and trade data and with case studies of Chile, Indonesia, the Democratic Republic of Congo, China, and Peru. This descriptive evidence is consistent with the view that these outcomes are structural but not uniform, and that context shapes how tightly the lock-in binds. We conclude with policy responses that target each link of the lock-in and argue that they must be combined, because no single measure is sufficient on its own.

candidates.title: Do trusting regions vote for Green parties? A post-materialist values channel in 21st-century Europe
candidates.abstract: While previous studies link social capital to environmental attitudes, we take a step further and ask whether trust translates into actual behaviour â€” voting for a Green party. We propose a post-materialist values channel through which social capital relates to Green electoral support, and examine it across European regions in one of the first studies of trust and observed electoral behaviour. Unlike most work, which relates survey-based attitudes to survey-based vote intentions, our dependent variable is real behaviour: the regional vote share of 41 European Green parties in parliamentary elections (2002â€“2022), matched with regional trust indicators from the European Social Survey. The estimations confirm our hypothesis that higher trust relates positively to Green electoral results, with highly statistically significant and robust associations for social, institutional, and international trust. A one-standard-deviation rise in regional social trust is associated with a 0.1-standard-deviation rise in Green support. In addition, post-materialist attitudes appear more important than redistributive preferences, and these associations are stronger in high-trust regions. This suggests that, in 21st-century Europe, typical Green voters are less oriented towards the left than previously thought and more driven by post-materialist values.

candidates.title: The Electoral Effects of U.S. Prison Construction
candidates.abstract: From 1980 to 2000, the United States opened over 400 prisons, a rapid expansion of carceral capacity mirroring the punitive turn in public policy and public opinion. Yet few studies have examined the impact of prison construction on nearby residents and their political behavior. We develop a theoretical model tracing how prison openings affect economic, attitudinal, and electoral outcomes in surrounding communities. Using modern difference-in-difference methods and a novel county-level dataset covering forty years of prison openings, we find that prison construction decreases county-level vote share for Republican candidates, especially if Republicans represented the county during prison construction. Drawing on analyses of economic outcomes and prison bond measure support, we argue that voters sanction issue-owning Republican candidates for negative economic externalities and turn against funding for prisons. These findings challenge conventional wisdom about the political economy of prisons and have implications for how we understand contemporary expansions of carceral capacity.

candidates.title: Secularization Backlash: A Tale of Two Coups
candidates.abstract: This paper examines how past ideological state-building constrains future reform. In Pakistan, General Zia’s regime (1977–1988) embedded religious identity into law, education, and political life. Two decades later, General Musharraf (1999–2008) sought to reverse course by pursuing a competing vision of national renewal. Leveraging a newly assembled district-level panel spanning half a century and an array of difference- in-differences strategies, we show that liberalizing reforms under Musharraf triggered a severe backlash in districts previously Islamized by Zia’s policies, reflected in heightened political violence and rising electoral support for Islamist parties. Evidence supports a mechanism In which Zia’s Islamization increased exposure to religious extremism among school-age cohorts. Relative to earlier cohorts, these cohorts were more likely to attend madrasas (religious seminaries) teaching more hard line religious doctrine. The districts that later display backlash also exhibit higher early marriage rates among girls, slower gains in female literacy, and greater Qur’an readership, consistent with a reorientation toward more conservative social and political preferences. These findings suggest that when states fuse Islamist ideology with governance, they create enduring constraints on future policy change. Past ideological investments can thus limit the effectiveness of later efforts at secularization or reform.

candidates.title: Fiscal integration as a Pareto improvement
candidates.abstract: Fiscal integration in a currency union is generally understood as a transfer from fiscally strong to fiscally weak countries. I show that this changes when common debt is paired with a non-defaultable common tax, even if national debt remains defaultable. The risky country gains from intertemporal trade: it receives a grant financed by a perpetual obligation it discounts more heavily than lenders do. The cost to the safe member is second-order and the tax removes it by insuring imperfectly correlated cycles rather than transferring resources in expectation. The calibration delivers a narrow Pareto-improving region: the tax that eliminates the risky country’s perverse incentive to default is negligible, while the tax that compensates the safe country is an order of magnitude larger. Joint spending on a public good expands the region and reverses that ordering: the safe country gains even before the common budget balances. JEL Classification: F34, F36, F45, H63, H87

candidates.title: Manufacturing Renaissance Meets Time-Inconsistent Tariffs -- by Christoph Boehm, Andrei A. Levchenko, Wei Xiang
candidates.abstract: We analyze optimal tariffs in a dynamic version of the Venables (1987) framework with a time-to-build lag in firm creation. In this environment, trade protection is driven by the desire to increase firm creation at home at the expense of the foreign trade partner. When firm creation takes time, the benefits of protection accrue in the future, whereas the costs in the form of higher consumer prices occur immediately. Under certain parameterizations, a policymaker that can commit to a full time path of tariffs leaves trade unrestricted at date 0, and announces high tariffs coming on at a pre-specified future period. But there is a time inconsistency: the policymaker's short-run incentive is not to impose contemporaneous tariffs due to the adverse effect on prices. Thus, lack of commitment to future tariffs can preserve free(er) trade and derail a manufacturing renaissance.

candidates.title: Climate-Nutrition Policy Coverage and Implementation Provisions in National Documents of 10 Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Paired Document Analysis
candidates.abstract: Background: Climate change and malnutrition share causes, and governments should tackle them together. Few studies ask whether national policy documents link the two or contain the provisions needed to act on that link. A policy with no budget, owner, deadline, or consequence is hard to deliver. This matters most in low- and middle-income countries. We aimed to describe how fully national climate and nutrition documents cover eight policy domains, test whether fuller coverage goes with more implementation provisions, and find which provisions are most often missing. Method: We analyzed 21 national documents (10 nutrition, 11 climate) from 10 countries in Africa, Asia, the Pacific, and Latin America. Two reviewers scored each country on a coverage index (eight domains, 0 to 3 each; maximum 24) and a readiness index (six provisions, present or absent; maximum 6). A third researcher settled disagreements. Analyses were exploratory. Results: Median coverage was 14.5 and readiness 3.5. Monitoring appeared in all 10 countries, but only one had an accountability provision. Five had a dedicated budget. Financing was the weakest domain (mean 1.0 of 3). The indices correlated closely (ρ = .99), partly because they share anchors. A version with less overlap gave ρ = .90 (95% CI .56 to 1.00), the safer estimate. Conclusion: Countries describe how they will track progress, yet almost none say who answers when targets are missed. Governments revising these plans should add accountability and financing provisions. These findings concern policy text, mostly second-round NDCs, not delivery, and need testing against implementation data and newer documents.

candidates.title: Closing the Gender Pension Gap – Labor Supply and Welfare Effects of Progressive Pensions
candidates.abstract: Progressive pension supplements mechanically reduce the gender pension gap because women receive lower pensions on average. However, labor supply responses may offset these gains and create fiscal externalities. Using German administrative data, we analyze the distributional and welfare effects of a progressive pension supplement. We find no labor supply responses during working life, but small effects on women’s employment and earnings in retirement. The supplement reduces the gender income gap by about two percent, with sizable heterogeneity across pension levels. The marginal value of public funds is 0.83. Means-testing based on household income improves welfare even with low redistributive preferences.

candidates.title: Assessing the Distributional and Fiscal Impacts of Cyprus's 2026 Personal Income Tax Reform
candidates.abstract: This paper assesses the distributional and fiscal implications of Cyprus's 2026 personal income tax (PIT) reform. The analysis is motivated by the fact that major tax reforms can reallocate disposable income across households with heterogeneous consumption and saving behavior, and different balance-sheet characteristics. From a central bank perspective, such distributional shifts are relevant because they can influence the strength and composition of monetary policy transmission (cash-flow versus financial channels) and may interact with household leverage, with potential implications for financial stability. Using tax-benefit microsimulations combined with confidential household microdata, the effect of PIT bracket amendments and two income-dependent tax allowances (for dependent children and university students and for mortgage interest or rental expenses) is evaluated. The results indicate uneven gains across the income distribution. Given that a large share of taxpayers is below the pre-reform tax-free threshold (EUR19, 500), simulated gains for the bottom income groups are minimal. The largest gains accrue to upper-middle-income and high-income households, while lower-middle-income and mid-middle-income households experience relatively modest benefits. The estimated fiscal cost of the PIT measures included in the analysis is around EUR240 million. Alternative configurations of the upper PIT brackets could have reduced gains at the top of the income distribution and preserved fiscal space for other policy priorities.

candidates.title: From Reagan to Trump: Regional development traps and the remaking of American electoral politics
candidates.abstract: This paper examines the territorial reconfiguration of American electoral politics since the 1980s, tracing the remaking of Republican support from Reaganâ€™s 1984 landslide to Trumpâ€™s three presidential campaigns (2016, 2020, 2024). Drawing on panel data for every presidential election from 1984 to 2024 across 722 commuting zones, we test whether regional development traps, defined as enduring economic underperformance, explain both the shift from Democrats to Republicans and the Republicansâ€™ internal realignment. Mundlak/Correlated Random Effects estimates show backlash is overwhelmingly driven by structural, not cyclical, decline. Short-term economic fluctuations do not predict Republican swing, while long-run territorial position does so decisively. Voters are not responding to recessions. They are registering alienation from an economic order that has failed their communities for a generation. Trumpâ€™s gains concentrated in places persistently left behind, whose peripheral position has become entrenched.

candidates.title: Constructing Measures in the Social Sciences: Best Practices and Common Pitfalls
candidates.abstract: Social scientists have long had access to sophisticated measurement models, but the instruments those models evaluate often receive far less care than the models themselves. Our aim is to close that gap by providing practical guidance for constructing valid self-report measures of latent constructs in sociology. We first establish a common terminology and an ideal four-phase construction process: defining the construct, developing an initial draft of the measure, empirical evaluation and iterative revision, and validation in an independent sample. We then identify six pitfalls that recur in applied work: imprecise construct definitions; conflating formative and reflective specifications; misuse of factor analysis, where global fit indices are treated as a summary verdict on scale quality; binary interpretations of measurement invariance tests; the neglected validation of single-item measures; and inattention to item-response quality. For each, we discuss the phases at which it arises, the consequences for substantive conclusions, and potential remedies. Throughout, political trust serves as a running example.

candidates.title: Geopolitical Tensions, Social Identity and the Fragmentation of the Global Economy
candidates.abstract: Geopolitical tensions threaten to fragment the global economy into rival blocs. As a driver of this fragmentation, we propose a demand-side channel grounded in social identity theory: consumers value goods partly by the political and economic values embodied in their origin. We embed this in a trade model with two countries that are similar in terms of political values and one dissimilar country, with the US, the EU and China as our benchmark example. We show that a geopolitical shock raising the salience of political over economic values diverts trade toward the similar pair and can also make a previously unattractive standards-harmonization agreement between them mutually beneficial. A subsequent estrangement of the similar pair, through diverging political values or trade-war measures, can reverse both effects and push the world economy from two blocs toward three. We also apply the framework to an estrangement of the US from the EU and Canada. Both a US divergence in political values and trade-war measures divert trade toward the EU-Canada pair, but only the former can make a previously unattractive EU-Canada agreement mutually beneficial.

candidates.title: From posts to proof: Classifying the evidentiary uses of social media traces in refugee status determination
candidates.abstract: Evidence is notoriously scarce in refugee status determination procedures. Digital traces from social media arise as a new form of evidence used by migration authorities and asylum claimants alike to support decision-making. Yet how exactly these traces factor into the evidentiary assessment of claims remains largely unaccounted for, especially in light of minimal precedence and procedural guidelines. With an empirical grounding in interview summaries from the Danish Refugee Appeals Board, this article’s contribution is two-fold. First, it identifies the evidentiary purposes of digital trace data from asylum claimants’ social media by developing a classification with four distinct clusters. These clusters identify four areas where digital traces from social media factor into the procedure: Establishing baseline information about the claimant, approximating exposure, corroborating or challenging claims about identity or past events, and identifying external conditions in the country of origin. Our classification reveals that digital traces from social media inform the evidentiary as sessment of claims in ways that extend towards assessments of credibility and risk of persecution. Second, it contributes to the literature on the use of digital traces as evidence in asylum decision making by placing the findings in the context of refugee law’s ‘fact-finding crisis’. We conclude that social media frequently arises as “silent evidence” that remains available to inform the background knowledge of decision-makers without explicitly being accounted for as evidence.

candidates.title: Greed versus Fear: Optimal Time-Consistent Taxation with Default
candidates.abstract: This paper studies optimal time-consistent distortionary taxation with default. The government taxes labor income or issues non-contingent debt to finance an exogenous stochastic stream of fiscal shocks. Debt can be repudiated subject to default costs. Optimal policy is characterized by two opposing incentives that capture the double lack of commitment to old tax policies and to repaying debt, respectively: an incentive to postpone taxes by issuing more debt for the future (â€œGreedâ€ ), and an incentive to tax more currently to avoid punishing default premia (â€œFearâ€ ). A Generalized Euler Equation captures these forces and determines the optimal back-loading or front-loading of tax distortions. Even with small default risk, tax-smoothing and debt issuance are substantially limited when short-term debt is available. The same mechanisms operate in environments with long-term debt, but debt serves more as a fiscal absorber.

candidates.title: Party factions and candidate selection
candidates.abstract: We study how political parties share power internally by analyzing the allocation of list positions to different factions. We develop a theory of intra-party bargaining in which list positions shape the mobilization efforts of party activists in different factions. Our results allow us to link observable patterns in list allocations to the importance of consensus in intra-party negotiations. We empirically evaluate these predictions using data from Norwegian municipal elections. We exploit a wave of municipal mergers to identify candidates' geography-based factional affiliations. In line with our theory's functionalist logic and consensus-based bargaining, smaller factions are over-compensated in both safe and contested list positions, but more so in safe positions. Our theoretical and empirical results show that parties can promote consensus among their factions while maintaining mobilization incentives, indicating that equality and efficiency within a political organization can be simultaneously achieved.

candidates.title: Beyond the Father: Frankenstein as an Economic and Political Allegory, from Godwinian perfectibility to Malthusian limits
candidates.abstract: This article argues that Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein renders visible a fundamental problem for understanding the limits of political economy: the logic of unintended consequences. It reads the novel as a narrative elaboration of this problem within the intellectual horizon of the debate between William Godwin and Thomas Robert Malthus on the limits of human and social perfectibility. Shelley articulates this problem through two complementary planes. On the one hand, Victor Frankenstein represents deliberate intervention whose effects exceed the agent’s capacity for foresight and control. On the other, the Creature embodies individual action that, through interaction with the social environment, generates consequences contrary to its own ends. Although these dimensions operate through distinct mechanisms, they generate the same type of outcome. This dual articulation is not incidental; it emerges within her intellectual horizon, shaped by the debate between Godwin and Malthus, which brought to the fore the limits of human perfectibility and the tensions inherent in social interaction. Within the history of economic thought, this problem cuts across distinct traditions. One, associated with deliberate intervention, concerns the organisation of economic life under conditions of imperfect knowledge, while the other, linked to social interaction, extends from Bernard Mandeville to Adam Smith in analysing unintended outcomes arising from individual action. Frankenstein brings these two analytical logics into a unified frame. In doing so, the novel reveals a fundamental limit of purposive action, the difficulty of maintaining control over processes whose dynamics exceed the agent’s capacity for anticipation. Rather than illustrating an external principle, Frankenstein articulates, from within, a problem central to political economy, the limits of control under conditions of complexity and uncertainty.

candidates.title: Constructing an Elite: Identity and Boundary Work on a Darknet Drug Market
candidates.abstract: This article examines how users of Cebulka, the largest Polish-language darknet drug cryptomarket, construct and negotiate their online identities. Utilizing nineteen in-depth interviews with vendors and buyers, the research employs a qualitative methodology informed by reflexive thematic analysis, social identity theory, the SIDE model. Based on the data, five themes are developed: 1) lower perceived physical and social danger; 2) greater knowledge, technical competence, and access to higher-quality products; 3) care for others; 4) higher social status; and 5) separation between darknet personas and offline lives. Across these themes, Cebulka’s users collectively framed themselves as an elite community distinct from street-level market participants. Thus the cryptomarket operates not just as a transactional space but as a site of identity work and symbolic boundary drawing—one that inverts the context collapse and algorithmic datafication typical of the visible web. These findings carry implications for harm reduction, drug policy, and the sociology of online communities, while highlighting the ambivalent, exclusionary character of the market’s technical barriers.

candidates.title: A Framework for Integrating Climate Goals into Trade Agreements
candidates.abstract: A critical tension in global governance is that trade agreements have evolved largely in isolation from climate policy. This paper shows that the two domains generate systematic cross-externalities: larger gains from trade are associated with greater climate externalities imposed on partners, while linking carbon taxes to trade agreements produces distributive externalities that undermine the balance of trade concessions. To address this tension, we present a framework to integrate harmonized carbon pricing into the WTO subject to institutional and political-feasibility constraints. We explore two linkage designs. The first is a centralized Climate Fund, where all members apply a common demand-side carbon tax and contribute a portion of the revenues to the fund, capped by fiscal constraints. The Fund then reallocates these contributions to balance the tax burden across countries, subject to informational constraints. Quantitative analysis shows that even a simple fund allocation rule can sustain a carbon price of $138 per ton of CO2, reducing global emissions by 54%. The main binding constraint is informational: knowing the precise incidence of the carbon tax across countries ex ante would raise the feasible price to $265. The second is a decentralized design without transfers. Each member meets a carbon tax revenue floor but retains full discretion over its mix of demand-side and supply-side taxes. Energy exporters choose supply-side taxes while energy importers opt for demand-side taxes. These choices organically balance the tax burden and yield a 47% reduction in global emissions, almost rivaling the centralized Climate Fund.

candidates.title: Same Destination, Different Eyes: FDI and Trade Responses to Media Coverage of Geopolitical Risk
candidates.abstract: Existing measures of geopolitical risk are country-level and assume that all investors face the same risk in a given destination. This paper constructs a directional, bilateral geopolitical risk index that captures how the domestic media of each source country report on geopolitical conflicts involving each destination country. Using GDELT news data, the index covers more than 200 source and destination countries at a monthly frequency. We combine the index with project-level data on greenfield FDI and product-level trade data, and exploit variation across source countries for the same destination and period while controlling for destination-specific shocks. Source countries whose media place greater emphasis on a destination's geopolitical risk subsequently announce more greenfield projects there: a one-standard-deviation increase in the index is associated with a 7% increase in new projects. This suggests that firms may read such coverage as a signal of future market-access frictions and localize production in advance. Consistent with this interpretation, the association is concentrated in projects serving the host market and in sectors that depend on local demand, and is absent among politically aligned country pairs. By contrast, higher risk coverage is followed by a short-lived decline in imports, driven by severe conflicts, while exports do not respond.

candidates.title: De facto voting power and the value of voting rights
candidates.abstract: We document high persistence in shareholder turnout, creating predictable differences in effective voting power across firms. Accordingly, firms with lower turnout exhibit higher voting premia. For identification, we exploit the 2010 NYSE Rule 452 amendment eliminating broker authority over uninstructed shares as a shock to turnout in director elections. Further, we show that low turnout predicts contentious governance events where shareholder influence is more valuable, and that the negative voting premium-turnout relation is stronger when such events are more likely. Results indicate that investors price de facto voting power and that persistent shareholder participation shape the value of corporate control.

candidates.title: Dynamic Identification of Sovereign Facilitators in International Corporate Tax Avoidance
candidates.abstract: International corporate tax avoidance is facilitated by sovereign jurisdictions that function as tax havens, financial secrecy havens, or offshore financial centres. The active policies of these jurisdictions potentially erode the tax basis of other countries, create an uneven playing field for domestic and multinational firms, and undermine international fiscal cooperation. However, the definition and identification of such sovereign facilitators of tax avoidance is --in both policy documents and academic literature-- surrounded by a lack of agreement. Traditional lists of tax havens are seldom updated, have no time variance, and often ignore tax havens among rich countries. This paper proposes the Joint Dynamic Identification Framework (JDIF), a standardised method that simultaneously identifies tax havens, financial secrecy havens, and offshore financial centres. Using only five statistical indicators makes it easy to apply this identification tool. We present a full-fledged proof-of-concept, covering the period 2001-2022 and more than 200 jurisdictions. The JDIF method shows that the pattern of border-crossing corporate tax avoidance is highly dynamic. Individual jurisdictions sometimes change their specialisation in tax avoidance networks. The JDIF method reveals shifting patterns between groups of tax-avoidance-facilitating jurisdictions and generates data that can be used in network analysis. Several robustness tests show the validity of our findings and demonstrate its policy relevance.

candidates.title: Free to roam, hard to tax? The tax implications of digital nomad visas in the EU
candidates.abstract: A growing number of countries have introduced Digital Nomad Visas (DNVs) to accommodate the rise of location-independent remote work, often paired with tax incentives. Using simulation analysis, this paper examines the effective tax burden of digital nomads under DNVs in the EU. Results show that tax burdens are sensitive to host country choice, double tax treaty provisions, and duration of stay, with the 183-day threshold proving critical. Tax planning can generate substantial tax savings for digital nomads who relocate strategically. This raises tax fairness concerns, as host countries may bear costs associated with digital nomads without proportionate income tax revenue.

candidates.title: The Effects of Monetary Policy on Macroeconomic Expectations: High-Frequency Evidence from Prediction Markets -- by Eric T. Swanson, Wang Renxuan, Yanbin Wu
candidates.abstract: When the Federal Reserve raises interest rates, standard macroeconomic models and VARs predict that output, employment, and inflation should fall over the next several quarters. However, monthly-frequency professional macroeconomic forecast revisions are sometimes positively correlated with Fed interest rate changes, leading to a debate about what could explain these puzzling correlations. We bring to bear new high-frequency data on this question from macroeconomic event contracts traded on Kalshi, a CFTC-licensed, U.S.-based event trading exchange and prediction market. These high-frequency event contracts allow us to isolate and estimate the effects of monetary policy and other announcements on Kalshi market-implied macroeconomic expectations. Our results are consistent with standard transmission channels from monetary policy to the macroeconomy, with little or no role for a “Fed Information Effect”.

candidates.title: Immigration and Crime
candidates.abstract: The relationship between immigration and crime is one of the most salient issues in public discourse. Despite widespread public concern, most studies find no evidence that immigration increases crime rates in host countries. This article reviews recent empirical evidence on the relationship between immigration and crime. Rather than offering an exhaustive survey, it focuses on recent and seminal contributions, highlighting emerging trends and research frontiers. In particular, the article discusses how immigration policies can mediate the relationship between immigration and crime. It also discusses research on crimes against immigrants, a topic that has attracted increasing scholarly interest but remains largely neglected in public discourse. Finally, given the substantial gap between public perception and the empirical evidence, the article reviews research on immigration and crime perception.

candidates.title: Universities as Incubators of Mass Uprising -- by Sultan Mehmood, Ahmed Mushfiq Mobarak
candidates.abstract: We link high-frequency geocoded protest data during Bangladesh’s 2024 Monsoon Revolution, Facebook measures of protest activity and social connectivity, university enrollment and demographics to establish: (1) student-linked protests precede off-campus mobilization; (2) student concentration predicts both on- and off-campus protest, while non-student youth, educated adults, urbanization, and locations of “placebo” universities authorized but not yet operating do not; and (3) social connectivity to student protest locations predicts off-campus diffusion one week later. Universities appear to incubate mass uprising by making dissent visible, coordinated, and capable of spreading beyond campus. Such patterns are also evident in U.S. Vietnam War protests and in global data. That universities facilitate broader political mobilization can explain why governments often seek to restrict student activism.

candidates.title: Dividend Taxes and the Limits of the New View
candidates.abstract: The new view of dividend taxation bundles three logically distinct claims: capitalisation, that a permanent dividend tax is impounded in share values; the Auerbach prediction, that the firm's real retention and investment decision is unchanged; and the King criterion, that the tax does not enter the cost of capital. In a frictionless two-period general-equilibrium economy with an all-equity firm and a power production technology, we show that the three claims hold under progressively stronger conditions. Capitalisation always holds, since the tax cancels from the firm's investment first-order condition, and in partial equilibrium Fisher separation delivers the new view in full. The failures are general-equilibrium phenomena that sort by margin: a subsistence level of consumption in otherwise standard HARA preferences breaks the Auerbach prediction for any technology, whereas the King criterion fails only when returns to capital are also decreasing, with a magnitude proportional to the product of technological curvature and the subsistence level. These breaks are uncompensated income effects, not substitution distortions: a revenue-neutral lump-sum rebate restores neutrality for any preferences and any technology. No friction is needed, only the curvature of preferences and technology and the breakdown of Fisher separation when the firm is the sole store of value. The all-equity assumption is inessential; under risk, by contrast, an asymmetric loss offset distorts the price of risk, a substitution distortion that no lump-sum rebate can repair.

candidates.title: Accounting for migrant definitions improves global migration modeling
candidates.abstract: Reliable estimates of international migrant populations matter for migration policy, social cohesion, and integration. Most countries define migrants as foreign-born population, but about one in five defines them by citizenship. Under the citizenship definition, migrants are foreign residents who exit the migrant stock by acquiring the host country's citizenship. Existing migration models apply the country-of-birth definition to all countries due to data availability and reduced modeling complexity. We present a stochastic model that consistently applies the migrant definition of each country and represents citizenship acquisition as a probabilistic process based on legal residence requirements. Across 192 countries from 1990 to 2020, we find that accounting for migrant definitions improves the agreement of simulation results with UN reported migrant stocks. The normalized error against reported stocks decreases from 35.1% to 23.0% in Africa and from 18.1% to 13.6% in Asia, the two world regions where the citizenship-based migrant definition is most common. In lower-middle- and upper-middle-income destinations, the 95% prediction intervals cover the reported stocks in all reference years. Results in regions that apply a country-of-birth migrant definition remain essentially unchanged. Where reported figures are available, estimated citizenship acquisitions are plausibly represented within our model. Our results show that migrant definitions, and the citizenship laws behind them, shape the dynamics of migrant populations and not only how these populations are counted. The approach is transferable to other global migration models and can be refined as citizenship acquisition data become available for non-OECD countries.

candidates.title: Physicians' Occupational Licensing and the Quantity-Quality Trade-off
candidates.abstract: Occupational licensing is a widespread quality regulation that potentially increases the quality of labor but reduces its quantity. We provide a theoretical framework to empirically quantify this trade-off in public hospitals, where both clinical quality and physician shortages are critical concerns. Using quasi-exogenous variation driven by a recent and unprecedented migration of physicians to Chile, together with growth in domestic medical schools, we show that more physicians improve patient outcomes, while lower-quality physicians—as measured by licensing exam performance—worsen them. Incorporating these findings into our theoretical framework, we evaluate the implications of locally changing the stringency of the licensing policy.

candidates.title: Governance Regimes, Economic Mobility, and the Composition of Public Investment: Evidence from the Democratization of Villages in India -- by Andrew D. Foster, Mark R. Rosenzweig
candidates.abstract: We develop a quantifiable general-equilibrium model of village governance, motivated by India’s democratization, to study how political institutions shape public goods provision and economic development. The model features two groups, landowners and landless workers, with different preferences over public goods such as irrigation, schools, and employment programs. Households from both groups can enter nonfarm entrepreneurship, but face credit-dependent entry costs. We compare oligarchy, where landowners control public goods decisions, with democracy, where electoral competition determines policy based on the relative sizes of the two groups. The calibrated model predicts that democratization’s effects on public goods and growth are not uniform; they depend on population composition and the ease of occupational mobility through access to credit. Using a 37-year village-level panel from India (1971–2006) and exploiting variation in democratization driven by state and national reforms, we find strong support for these predictions. Financial intermediation shifts landless households’ preferences from wage-enhancing policies toward schooling, increasing nonfarm business entry. As a result, democracy provides fewer schools than oligarchy when credit is unavailable, but more schools when credit is accessible. We also show that transfers to the landless increase schooling under democracy but reduce it under oligarchy. These findings highlight how governance structures and economic conditions jointly determine the effectiveness of development policies.

candidates.title: Political Incentives in Local Tax Setting: Evidence from the German Property Tax Reform
candidates.abstract: Local governments’ discretion over tax rates may be used strategically when politicians perceive that a tax burden falls differently across voter groups. We study this mechanism in the context of Germany’s property tax reform, which created exogenous variation in the tax across voter groups and municipalities by allowing states to adopt different property valuation models. Some federal states implicitly set a higher tax for rental properties than for comparable owner-occupied units. We show that, over an average post-announcement period of 3.6 years, municipal tax multipliers increased by 15 percentage points more when two conditions were met: municipalities were governed by homeowner-friendly parties and were located in states where tenants will face a higher tax base per square meter. By identifying political drivers behind sharp increases in German property tax multipliers in recent years, we provide causal evidence that higher-level governments’ tax-base choices change the electoral incentives governing local tax rates.

candidates.title: Diversity in school and friendships in adulthood: Evidence from West Germany's guest worker era
candidates.abstract: This paper investigates the long-term association between exposure to descendants of guest workers in school and native German students' friendships in adulthood. Beginning in 1955, millions of guest workers migrated to West Germany, resulting in significant demographic shifts. Using data from the German Socio-Economic Panel (SOEP), this study focuses on Germans who completed secondary school between 1975 and 1990. The results suggest that individuals experiencing inter-ethnic contact in school are more likely to have foreign friends in adulthood, with this association being strongest for individuals who grew up in rural areas. Possible channels are a change in attitudes, likely due to a reduction in prejudice, and sorting into more urban regions with more opportunities for intergroup contact in adulthood. The results indicate that exposure to diversity in school may be associated with lasting differences in attitudes and behavior.

candidates.title: Tax Productivity and Economic Development: A Quantitative Macroeconomic Analysis
candidates.abstract: This paper examines the role of government capacity to collect taxes in driving economic development. We first draw on a new macro-historical database to document that tax collections relative to tax administration expenditures rise sharply with GDP per capita. We then interpret this finding in a neoclassical growth model with a tax administration sector in which labor inputs are required to raise tax revenues. Countries differ in their levels of tax productivity, capturing how effectively labor is used to raise taxes, as well as their levels of productivity in creating consumption and investment goods. Governments use tax revenues to provide public capital that complements private factors in production and to make transfers. Quantitatively, our model predicts that increases in tax productivity in low-income economies can raise GDP per capita substantially more than suggested by Hulten’s theorem.

candidates.title: Insult Politics in the Age of Social Media
candidates.abstract: This paper studies the production of offensive content by politicians on Twitter/X. Applying AI-based methods to the universe of tweets posted by members of the U.S. Congress (2017 - 2022), I measure the returns to offensive communication both in terms of online engagement and electoral support. I document that posting toxic tweets generates a sizable engagement premium and that these gains decrease with politicians' baseline toxicity. To examine how voters respond to offensive speech, I link the timing of toxic tweets to a large-scale electoral survey. Using an event study design around days marked by sharp spikes in representatives' toxic tweeting activity, I find that voting intentions for the politician increase in the following week. The increase is concentrated among ideologically aligned voters, while opponents display lower electoral support, widening the partisan voting gap. These findings highlight the presence of both online and electoral incentives to the production of offensive communication, which comes at the expense of growing polarization.

candidates.title: Returnees Reproducing Hegemony in the Digital Age: Off/Online Attitudes of the Western-born in Vietnam
candidates.abstract: **This paper has been accepted for publication in Southeast Asia: A Multidisciplinary Journal published by Emerald Publishing Limited** This paper examines how ethnically similar, yet culturally different ethnic return migrants use information communication technologies to reproduce and challenge Western hegemonies in their ancestral homeland. Drawing on 31 online in-depth interviews with 2nd and 2.5 generation Vietnamese living in Viet Nam, from 11 disparate Western countries, it explores the social-cultural, economic, and political (dis)advantages engendered within this hierarchically stratified, multiple-minority coethnic group. Employing Anibal Quijano’s concept of global coloniality, coethnic hierarchies are examined in the ethnic homeland. As such it asks, how are hierarchies among these coethnics played out off/online? To what extent are Western hegemonies reproduced off/online by Western-born ethnic return migrants and what are the tensions within this cohort in off/online groups?

candidates.title: Political Liability Insurance for Campaign Promises
candidates.abstract: In liberal democracies, the inability of voters to enforce campaign pledges represents an agency problem, as politicians can make non-binding promises during elections without incurring ex ante costs. This paper introduces an economic model of mandatory liability insurance for political campaign promises. Under this framework, candidates running for office must obtain liability insurance for at least one quantifiable policy target. Insurance companies screen candidates and assess risks, setting individualized premiums paid by the candidates that reflect candidate credibility, expertise, and policy feasibility. Insurance details are disclosed to the electorate, providing voters with additional information. After the election, an independent evaluation body determines whether the promised thresholds have been met. If a promise is not fulfilled, the insurer pays financial compensation into a public fund. Political liability insurance thus offers a potential solution to the problem of unenforceable campaign promises, promoting a more transparent and accountable electoral process.

candidates.title: Global Entrepreneurial Talent Flows: Widely Funded, Selectively Successful?
candidates.abstract: Immigrant founders of US venture-backed startups exit successfully more often than native founders. Does this hold worldwide? Using career histories for 913, 226 founder-firm pairs in 213 countries (1990–2026), we compare founders who build abroad (expats) or return home after foreign experience (returnees) with comparable local founders in the same country. Both expats and returnees raise early funding more often globally. Expats' success premium, however, concentrates in the US (18 percent) and UK (26 percent), especially among those entering the US through graduate school, work, or direct founding. Returnees rarely show such a premium. Capital follows mobile founders across borders, but success follows them selectively.

candidates.title: Yet another sham election in Russia: The upcoming ballot for the ninth State Duma
candidates.abstract: So far, 2026 is not proving a good year for the Putin regime. The front line in Ukraine is barely moving, Ukrainian drones and missiles are striking targets deep inside Russian territory, the economy is faltering and public sentiment is deteriorating. Under these difficult conditions, the Kremlin administration has to engineer another victory for the ruling United Russia party, as the State Duma elections are due to take place from 18 to 20 September. Yet the Russian parliament is scarcely able to fulfil its function as a source of legitimacy in Putin's personalised dictatorship. This is evident both from the chronic weakness of the parties loyal to the regime and from the farcical circumstances surrounding the exclusion of the Yabloko party from the election.

candidates.title: Green Tastes, Beliefs, and Portfolios: Evidence from Synthetic Investors -- by Xindi He, Lubos Pastor
candidates.abstract: We use LLMs as synthetic survey respondents to elicit green tastes, return beliefs, portfolio allocations, and investment motives from 480 retail and 60 institutional investor identities. Compared with retail, institutions report weaker tastes yet greener portfolio tilts, citing outside pressure. A greener tilt therefore need not indicate a stronger taste for greenness. Retail tastes depend mostly on political affiliation, institutional tastes on type and geography. Beliefs differ across the three ESG dimensions, with high-governance portfolios expected to outperform. We reconstruct survey responses under 2014--2025 information environments using date-masked information modules shuffled across years. Tastes vary little over time, but beliefs about green portfolios become more pessimistic after 2020. The two reconstructed series relate to different real-world data: tastes to measures of green demand, beliefs to measures of attention.

candidates.title: A theory of migration (florimigration): habitus, post-material values, and the reflexive pursuit of flourishing lives
candidates.abstract: This paper develops a theoretical framework for understanding florimigration, a concept introduced here to describe well-being focused migration in which individuals prioritize post-material aspirations, including autonomy, self-actualization, and holistic flourishing, over economic security or survival. Drawing on Bourdieu’s conceptualizations of habitus and field, Inglehart’s theory of post-material value change, and Giddens’ reflexive project of the self, the framework conceptualizes florimigration as an embedded life decision shaped by the interplay between pre-reflexive dispositions, conscious biographical deliberation, and macro-level structural conditions. Migration is theorized as emerging from a fundamental tension between an individual’s reconfigured habitus and the doxa of the origin country, whose normative and institutional conditions remain incongruent with post-material value orientations. At the macro level, the realization of florimigration aspirations depends on the structural conductivity of both origin and destination countries, defined by the political, legal, and institutional conditions that enable or constrain international mobility.

candidates.title: Measuring Trade-Disruption Exposure: A Sanctions-Based Index and Its Validation Against Trade
candidates.abstract: Economic sanctions are a routine instrument of statecraft, yet exposure to trade-restrictive measures is hard to compare across countries and over time. We build a continuous target-year index of trade-disruption exposure from the dyadic trade-sanction records of the Global Sanctions Data Base, Release 5, encoding the direction and stringency of each active restriction and the breadth of the sanctioning coalition, and a trade-weighted version scaling each restriction by the sender's pre-sanction trade share. In a structural gravity model the graded index recovers what a binary indicator hides. A complete ban is associated with a fall in bilateral trade of about two thirds, a partial ban about a tenth, and the binary flag averages them. The continuous index also predicts large reductions in aggregate trade where the binary indicator is only marginal. Applied to national income the association is not identified, which we present as a cautionary limit of aggregate inference.

candidates.title: Saving for the Machines -- by Jesús Fernández-Villaverde
candidates.abstract: When machines can perform a growing share of tasks, growth depends on two margins: how the task structure affects the returns to accumulating machines, and how strongly capital accumulation responds to those returns. I argue that, in a standard task model, capital supply governs the size of the growth boom associated with automation, while the task structure sets the duration of this growth boom and the evolution of wages. I document how the same technology path that generates 11.7% annual growth when households choose their saving rate optimally delivers only 2.2% when the saving rate is fixed at the calibrated U.S. 2025 level of 23%. Therefore, slow growth might reflect too little capital accumulation instead of a technological bottleneck. Also, the saving rate rises mainly because automation raises the capital share, not because households become thriftier. Long yields price the growth boom: the ten-year real yield jumps from 5.1% to 13.6% on impact. In my benchmark calibration, hand-to-mouth households lose the equivalent of two-fifths to two-thirds of their consumption, while keeping them on trend temporarily costs at most a fifth of GDP.

candidates.title: The Laffer curve in action
candidates.abstract: The Laffer curve illustrates a principle understood since Adam Smith: beyond a certain point, raising a tax rate reduces the revenue it brings in. Overall tax revenue in the UK has risen as the tax burden has grown, but several individual taxes now appear to have been pushed into this 'prohibitive range'. Alcohol duty, tobacco duty and landfill tax were all expected to raise more money after rate rises. Instead, alcohol duty receipts fell despite significant inflation, real-terms tobacco duty revenue fell by 40% between 2021 and 2025 as smokers turned to the black market, and landfill tax now raises half as much in real terms as it did at its 2013 peak, while fly-tipping has reached record levels. Together, these three taxes yielded £5.2 billion less than the OBR projected. This points to an over-reliance on static models that fail to anticipate how people respond to excessive taxation. Pushing taxes too far not only loses revenue but creates huge opportunities for criminals, and the cost of dealing with them falls on the public.

candidates.title: The Net Present Value of the California Billionaire Tax Act
candidates.abstract: This paper examines the revenue and migration impact of the 2026 California Billionaire Tax Act, a one-time 5 percent tax on the worldwide net worth of individuals exceeding $1 billion. Using data from the Forbes Billionaire List, news reports detailing the residential real estate holdings of California billionaires, and public announcements of billionaire departures from the state, we estimate the behavioral response and associated revenue loss to this new tax using several different methodologies. Even before accounting for reductions in other tax bases such as the income tax, we estimate that the Act will collect approximately $30 billion (range $28 to 36 billion), less than a third of the $100 billion projected by Galle et al. (2025). This range accounts for the publicly confirmed taxpayer migration that has already eliminated nearly 30 percent of the Act's wealth tax base, applies a litigation-survival discount to the remaining base, and is validated by the wealth tax base elasticity literature. We estimate that California's billionaires contribute $3.3–5.8 billion annually in state income taxes. The present value of permanently lost income tax collections from departures more than offsets the one-time wealth tax revenue, yielding a net present value of negative $38.9 billion. Across 100, 000 simulated revenue and discount rate combinations, 85 percent of plausible outcomes produce a negative net present value of state revenues.

candidates.title: A Beckerian Theory of Taxation -- by Margaret Chen, Mikhail Golosov, Ilia Krasikov
candidates.abstract: We study taxation in matching environments in which both equilibrium sorting and the sharing of match surplus are endogenous. Tax reforms lead to complex adjustments in sorting and surplus sharing patterns across the whole economy. We develop a general approach for characterizing these equilibrium adjustments using matching elasticities, which are primitive objects that describe how agents' matching choices are affected by pecuniary payoffs in partial equilibrium. Applying this approach to a workhorse model of family formation, we first show that the sorting and surplus sharing responses are closely linked to complementarities in the creation of economic surplus, as first emphasized by Becker (1973). We then describe the effects of arbitrary tax reforms on tax revenues, the utilities of different agents, and social welfare; design tests to assess Pareto efficiency of existing tax systems; derive formulas that characterize optimal taxes; and propose numerical techniques to compute them. In a calibrated model, we find that optimal marginal tax rates are substantially lower and less progressive than in the Mirrleesian benchmark.

candidates.title: Aggregate-Surplus Maximizing Monetary Policy -- by David Baqaee, Ariel Burstein, Joao Guerreiro
candidates.abstract: We study optimal monetary policy in a general heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian (HANK) economy. Instead of maximizing a social welfare function, the policymaker maximizes the joint surplus of all households, without taking a stance on how that surplus should be distributed. This is the policy that maximizes resources left over if winners from reform were to compensate losers. We derive the approximate optimal policy using linear-quadratic methods. The quadratic objective function nests the standard New Keynesian loss function and adds losses from incomplete markets and heterogeneous labor wedges. We show that optimal policy is the sum of time-dependent and state-contingent components. When labor wedges are homogeneous, monetary policy cannot improve household insurance: the time-dependent component is zero, and optimal policy coincides with the representative-agent New Keynesian (RANK) benchmark. Departures from RANK arise from heterogeneous labor wedges. In that case, the time-dependent component temporarily alleviates incomplete-market distortions but vanishes over time. The state-contingent component solves a dual-mandate problem, as in RANK, but with a higher weight on output-gap stabilization relative to inflation stabilization. In a calibrated model, heterogeneous labor wedges raise this weight by about 37 percent. We also find that a dual mandate with this higher weight achieves almost all of the aggregate-surplus gains from the full optimal policy and requires no compensatory transfers between winners and losers.

candidates.title: State Child Tax Credits and Parental Labor Supply: Evidence from Staggered Adoption
candidates.abstract: States increasingly supplement the federal Child Tax Credit (CTC) with credits that vary in generosity, refundability, and earnings requirements. We examine changes in parental employment, labor force participation, and work hours following state CTC adoption using the Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS-ASEC), 2004–2026. Our preferred stacked difference-in-differences design includes 12 adopting states with complete event-time support and compares them with never-treated states and states that adopted after our evaluation window. Averaging over the first three post-adoption survey years, the estimated effect is 0.05 percentage points (SE 1.03) for employment and −0.46 points (0.82) for labor force participation; estimates for work hours are also close to zero. Across secondary specifications and CPS Basic Monthly analyses, extensive-margin estimates were similarly small. Larger simulated benefits are associated with fewer hours among employed parents, but the relationship is also evident before adoption and may partly reflect how benefits depend on earnings. Overall, the estimates provide little indication that state CTC adoption has substantially reduced parental employment, although meaningful effects in either direction cannot be ruled out under moderate departures from parallel trends.

candidates.title: The Quest for Freedom and Migration Aspirations: Evidence from the MENA Region
candidates.abstract: This article develops and empirically tests a theory of migration under repression. It argues that migration aspirations are shaped by perceived freedom repression and that such perceptions can make exit more attractive when voice appears blocked, risky, or ineffective. The theoretical framework yields four hypotheses, which we test using Arab Barometer data from 2021– 2024 covering about 34, 000 respondents in twelve Middle East and North Africa (MENA) countries. Empirically, we construct a Freedom Repression Index and examine how perceived repression shapes migration aspirations across different freedom dimensions and migration routes. Four findings stand out. First, perceived repression significantly increases migration aspirations, with substantive effects comparable to standard economic push factors. Second, the association is strongest for personal liberties, especially freedom of expression and freedom of religion, whereas restrictions on collective political rights such as protest are less strongly associated with migration aspirations. Third, repression shifts intentions toward irregular rather than regular migration routes. Fourth, this relationship is context-dependent: it is strongest in stable yet restrictive settings and weakens in conflict-affected contexts where insecurity dominates. By disaggregating freedom dimensions and distinguishing regular from irregular intentions, the article connects exit-voice theory to micro-level evidence and clarifies when, which, and how perceived repression shapes migration aspirations in the MENA region.

candidates.title: The Referendum in Italy: A Reconstruction Based on Its Numbers
candidates.abstract: This paper examines the evolution of referendums in Italy, from the institutional referendum of 1946 to the consultations held in 2026, through a historical and quantitative analysis of electoral results. The study investigates trends in voter turnout, quorum attainment, voting preferences, the main issues submitted to popular consultation, and the role of referendum promoters, highlighting changes in the relationship between citizens, political institutions, and instruments of direct democracy. The findings reveal a progressive decline in participation in abrogative referendums, particularly since the 1990s. Of the 77 abrogative referendum questions examined, only 39 reached the required quorum, while average voter turnout declined from 60.9% before 2000 to 34.4% in the subsequent period. The analysis also suggests that the increasing frequency of consultations, the complexity of certain referendum questions, and the political instrumentalization of referendums have contributed to weakening their effectiveness and their capacity to mobilize citizens. The paper further highlights the contrast between the fundamental role played by referendums in shaping Italy's major civil, social, and institutional transformations and the growing difficulties faced by this instrument in influencing political decision-making. Overall, the study offers a critical reflection on the future of direct democracy in Italy, emphasizing the importance of restoring meaningful popular participation and strengthening the relevance of referendum outcomes within democratic processes.

candidates.title: Public R&D and the Automation of Manufacturing: Evidence from the Space Race -- by Apoorva Babbar, Shawn Kantor, Alexander Whalley, Jingyuan Zeng
candidates.abstract: This paper examines how public research and development shaped the direction of technological change during the Cold War–era Space Race and its consequences for US manufacturing. While prior research has documented the effects of public R&D on innovation and economic growth, less is known about whether mission-oriented public investment directed innovation toward automation and how this affected labor markets. We exploit variation in exposure to NASA's Space Race investments across industries and locations to estimate the effects of public R&D on innovation and manufacturing outcomes from 1947 to 1992. Combining newly developed measures of automation in full-text patent data with historical evidence on government involvement in patenting, we show that NASA-sponsored patents are systematically more automation-intensive than non-NASA patents within the same technological classes. Industries and locations more exposed to Space Race activity experienced persistent declines in labor share, consistent with the diffusion of labor-saving technologies developed for space applications. In contrast, we find little evidence of systematic changes in skill composition. These findings show that mission-oriented public R&D can shape the direction of technological change and have lasting distributional consequences.

candidates.title: The Global Office: How Globalisation’s Frontier is Shifting from Factories to Offices -- by Richard Baldwin
candidates.abstract: This paper argues that globalisation’s frontier has shifted from manufacturing GVCs to services GVCs: from the Global Factory to the Global Office. While the Factory remains larger in gross trade, the Office is growing much faster. A heatmap of trade in intermediates shows that the Factory is bloc-shaped and dominated by China, whereas the Office is star-shaped and dominated by America. Gravity estimates show that distance matters less for Office exports, but time zones matter more: each hour of time-zone separation reduces Office exports by roughly 4%, while having no effect on Factory exports. Importantly, all of the world’s export-linked net job creation between 2008 and 2022 occurred in digitally delivered services rather than manufacturing, and trade-linked service jobs command higher average pay globally. The Factory-to-Office shift is also reshaping development. Most emerging economies have seen export-led growth tilt towards services, but their service exports are not yet large enough to drive overall GDP growth the way manufacturing did historically. The big picture is that globalisation’s second unbundling is running out of steam even as its third unbundling is powering ahead. The paper, which raises more questions than it answers, closes with the conjecture that the future of trade is services.

candidates.title: Coase Meets Negishi: Property Rights, Welfare Weights, and Distributional Consequences in Climate Economics -- by Simon F. Lang, Matthew D. Gordon, Matthew J. Kotchen
candidates.abstract: We develop a property-rights based approach for defining welfare weights in economic models of climate change. Whether there is a "right to pollute" or a "right to no pollution" is increasingly contested in legislatures, courts, and international climate negotiations. We show how these notions of property rights can provide the basis for "Coasean welfare weights" that are applicable in multilateral public goods settings. Distributional questions are addressed through positive analysis, conditional on property rights, rather than normative views about redistribution. The implied transfers are consistent with a bargained solution over the net benefits of addressing climate change and reflect the value of property rights over emissions. The approach defines efficient allocations that generate Pareto improvements, in contrast to commonly used Negishi weights. We implement the approach in a global integrated assessment model to quantify what countries have at stake in ongoing political and legal debates about emissions-related property rights.

candidates.title: The Returns to Temporary Migration: Experimental Evidence from the H-2A Program
candidates.abstract: In 2024, 315, 000 H-2A temporary seasonal work visas were issued to agricultural workers in the US. The H-2A program is controversial: earnings are high, but critics argue that workers face poor working and living conditions and that families bear the costs of separation. We randomize H-2A seasonal visas for Mexican workers. During a single US season, migrants earn more than USD 16, 000 and send 70% of these earnings to origin households. Living standards in Mexico rise: food security increases, the probability of living in poverty falls by 10 percentage points, and families invest in home improvements, durable assets, and debt reduction, with little investment in businesses or productive assets. Migration has spillovers onto the household: the mental health of household respondents worsens and they avoid higher-risk situations such as walking at night, and intra-household dynamics change. Migrants generally report satisfaction with H-2A jobs and contracts, all report that they would migrate again, and 85% do so the following season.
